data.title: This Thanksgiving, be grateful for James Madison
data.description:
In both of his terms, and especially over the last two years, President Trump has stress-tested the Constitution in ways we didn’t imagine possible. But James Madison did.

There are a number of constitutional safeguards we have come to regard as quaint, or even obsolete, like the Third Amendment, forbidding the quartering of troops. But as Madison foresaw, these are now coming into their own, precisely when they are most needed.

Take the grand jury requirement in the Fifth Amendment. In 2016, federal prosecutors were unable to get grand juries to issue indictments only six times out of more than 150,000 attempts. But things are different now. Prosecutors might be able to get a grand jury to indict a ham sandwich, but not, as it turns out, a Subway sandwich.

One of the defining features of the Trump Department of Justice is its frequent grand jury face-plants. Time and time again, the Justice Department has sought to bring politically motivated cases designed to punish Trump’s enemies. And time and time again, grand juries have protected innocent people from the president’s wrath.

There’s Cassidy Hutchinson, who bravely testified about what happened at the White House on Jan. 6, 2021, during the Capitol Hill attacks. There is Letitia James, the state prosecutor who had the audacity to enforce her state’s elections laws, escaped indictment not once but twice for bogus charges of mortgage fraud. And let’s not forget the six members of Congress, all veterans, who made a video encouraging service members to follow the law and refuse illegal orders. That’s just a partial list.

It turns out we only thought the grand jury requirement was useless because it was working. Indictments were easy to get because prosecutors were rigorously ethical about only bringing cases they knew had merit. The minute U.S. attorneys began substituting politics for the rule of law, the grand jury came into its own and began doing what it was always intended to do: short-circuit efforts to use the justice system as a tool of oppression.

Madison was also way ahead of Trump when it comes to the latter’s efforts to intimidate the incoming Congress over its planned schedule of investigations into the last two years of White House sponsored legal and ethical mayhem.

It couldn’t be more clear that these efforts have everything to do with politics and nothing to do with justice. A letter filled with Native American stereotypes directed to Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) by Aaron Reitz, U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas, ordered her to preserve documents and threatened her with sanctions if she didn’t. “You appear eager to wield your future gavel like a tomahawk, hunting for the scalps of President Trump’s private associates,” he wrote. Similar, though slightly less cringe-inducing, letters were sent to Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) and Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.).

But thanks to Madison and the speech and debate clause that he wrote into the Constitution, this is all performative nonsense. The clause provides that, “for any Speech or Debate in either House, [members of Congress] shall not be questioned in any other Place.” This is, in effect, a grant of absolute immunity for anything that members of Congress do while engaging in legislative activities — that includes conducting congressional investigations. Warren is free to take her gavel and — metaphorically, of course — beat Trump and his “private associates” bloody with it. There is absolutely nothing Reitz, Blanche or anyone else can do about it — at least, not constitutionally.

Of course, you never know with Trump. But if there is one line he could cross that would convince a dozen Republican senators to vote for conviction in an impeachment trial, arresting members of Congress for doing their jobs is probably it.

This doesn’t mean that America’s constitutional government doesn’t need a lot of emergency repairs. You can’t see bits of it falling off yet, but the Supreme Court is now a zombie institution. It is impossible to confirm a new Supreme Court justice unless the same party controls both the presidency and the Senate. That means a court operating at less than full strength, possibly for years at a time, and wild ideological swings when the political stars align so that several Supreme Court seats can be filled at once.

And that’s just one example. We must fix the presidential immunity problem, take steps to clean up the presidential pardon system, shore up the independence of the Department of Justice, and make a host of other reforms. After 240 years, that’s no surprise. Madison and the founders couldn’t think of everything, and they couldn’t have anticipated the complexities of the modern world. There’s no denying that some of their solutions are more suited to the 18th century than the 21st.

There is a lot of work ahead of us, and we can take nothing for granted. But the founders had excellent instincts. Despite unprecedented effort to subvert it, the constitutional democracy they built still works. As we head into Thanksgiving, that’s something both Republicans and Democrats can be thankful for.

Chris Truax is an appellate attorney and charter member of the Society for the Rule of Law.

data.title: Massie says GOP 'already in a minority' due to absences
data.description:
Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) on Thursday expressed concerns about his Republican colleagues being absent in the House calling them “the retirement caucus.”

“At one point this week, I counted … there were three or four more Democrats than there were Republicans,” Massie told host Kaitlan Collins during an appearance on CNN. “So, we’re technically already in a minority because of the attendance problem.”

His remarks come after the Republicans suffered significant losses in the midterm elections earlier this month, losing control of both chambers of Congress. Democrats secured big wins in battleground states, flipping GOP-held seats in Texas, Kanas, Maine, South Carolina and more recently, Mississippi and Alaska.

The absence of Republicans, Massie said, could be because a lot of them “are looking for jobs.”

“I lost my election in May. I’ve had a lot of time to think about what to do next,” he told Collins. “These folks, two weeks ago, they found out that what they thought was an annuity, that they would be in Congress forever, was not gonna happen anymore.”

“So I think there are a lot of people scrambling and thinking of how to take care of their families and whatnot going forward,” the outgoing lawmaker added.

The Kentucky Republican has sparred with his party and colleagues in the past, most recently spearheading an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Massie introduced six articles of impeachment against Hegseth over what he called abuse of power.

Last week, however, House Republicans voted to shelf the impeachment measure in a tight 211-204 vote.

When asked about potential consequences around the absences Thursday, Massie called it “dangerous.”

“The Democrats could actually take control of the House if he tries to hold session when there’s more Democrats than there were Republicans,” he said, referring to Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La).

Johnson also recently noted that “attendance is a great frustration for me right now,” according to CNN.

data.title: Live updates: Trump to brief on China summit; GOP at odds over reconciliation
data.description:
President Trump, fresh from his trip to Asia, is set to brief reporters on his trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Trump touted the rare summit as “Great and Highly Consequential” in a post online following the meeting. Earlier Thursday, the trio announced that the talks yielded a symbolic “declaration toward peace.”

Meanwhile, Senate Republicans are increasingly at odds over the Trump administration’s push for a $350 billion Pentagon funding package. Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) warned that the reconciliation process could expose deep divisions within the GOP over Medicaid cuts enacted last year.

Some lawmakers are eager to revisit the healthcare reductions, while others fear reopening the debate could unravel key provisions of Trump’s signature tax law. Hill Insiders can learn more here.

On Thursday, Senate Republicans blocked another war powers resolution that would restrict further military operations in Iran. The upper chamber did advance the bipartisan permitting reform bill though, sending it to the House.

A federal district court in Virginia will also hear arguments Friday on a lawsuit seeking to prevent the construction of Trump’s proposed 250-foot triumphal arch. The hearing comes two days after a federal judge extended the block on construction.

Trump will host a reception in the afternoon and hold signing time. First lady Melania Trump, whose docuseries premiered late Thursday on Prime Video, will attend an arrival ceremony for the White House Christmas Tree.

Follow live below.

data.title: Magnitude 4.4 earthquake rocks Los Angeles County
data.description:
(KTLA) — An earthquake with a magnitude of 4.4 shook Los Angeles County early Friday morning.

According to the U.S. Geological Survey, the quake struck at 3:25 a.m. with an epicenter about a mile northwest of Commerce, at a depth of 16 kilometers.

Residents felt light shaking throughout Los Angeles County, but no injuries were immediately reported.

The quake also sent the Los Angeles Fire Department into its earthquake mode.

“Pursuant to protocol, the LAFD is now in earthquake mode, as personnel from all 106 neighborhood fire stations conduct a strategic survey by land, air and sea of their districts,” the Fire Department stated after the quake.

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass posted an update on X after the early-morning quake.

“While unsettling, there are no immediate reports of damage or operational impacts, including at LAX,” Bass posted.

The National Tsunami Warning Center has determined there is no tsunami threat.

Latest California Earthquakes. Please wait a moment for map to load.

What to do in an earthquake

During an earthquake, knowing the proper steps to protect yourself and minimize injury is crucial. The California Department of Public Health provides detailed guidelines on what to do during such events. Here are the key points:

Drop: Immediately drop down onto your hands and knees. This position prevents you from being knocked over and allows you to stay low and crawl to safety if necessary.

Cover: Use one arm to protect your head and neck, and, if possible, take shelter under a sturdy table or desk. If no shelter is available, get down next to an interior wall away from windows. Stay on your knees and bend over to protect vital organs.

Hold On: Hold onto your shelter until the shaking stops. Be prepared to move with it if it shifts.

data.title: Who gets to look presidential?
data.description:
On Nov. 2, Keisha Lance Bottoms knelt at her great-great-grandmother Betsy Peek’s grave in Crawfordville, Georgia, and wept. In 1860, Betsy’s husband, Sheppard, had appeared on a list of a white man’s possessions, valued at $1,400. On another surviving document, he signed with an “X.”

The next day, their descendant became the first Black woman elected governor of an American state.

Democrats seized the Senate and, before dawn Wednesday, the House. Texas elected its first Latina governor, Gina Hinojosa (D), and sent State Rep. James Talarico (D), a seminary graduate preaching a politics of love, to the Senate.

Dr. Annie Andrews (D), a pediatrician, won a Senate seat in South Carolina, where Democrats had not won since 1998. Kansas elected Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton, its first Democratic senator since 1932. In New Mexico, Deb Haaland became the first Native American woman elected governor. Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), Georgia’s first Jewish senator, won again. 

Abdul El-Sayed became the first Muslim elected to the Senate. In Michigan, Senator-elect El-Sayed addressed the vice president who would swear him in: “JD, habibi.” 

“Habibi” means my beloved in Arabic. Aimed at JD Vance, it had the mischievous bite of a Southern “bless your heart.” After months of attacks on his faith and name, El-Sayed had turned an Arabic word into the punchline of his victory speech. Then came the score of their college rivalry: “Wolverines 1, Buckeyes 0.” And to Trump, who had repeatedly mangled his name: “You can just go on and call me senator.” By Thursday, he had named his new political action committee: Habibi PAC.

With Ossoff’s precision, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s exuberant competence and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s (D-N.Y.) fire, the Democratic bench suddenly looked deeper and livelier than it had in years. Presidential speculation followed almost immediately. 

Amid the celebrations, I noticed whose futures we were imagining. 

Axios wrote that Ossoff had “vaulted into the top tier” of Democratic presidential prospects. In the same analysis, Bottoms appeared as a governor who could appoint a Democrat to the Senate if Ossoff or Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) won the White House. Axios had made the point in its original report of her victory and returned to it in subsequent coverage. 

The observation was sound, and either senator would be an exciting presidential prospect. But Bottoms had just ended 24 years of Republican rule in Georgia. Part of the national conversation about her future concerned the vacancy she might fill after a man reached the presidency. 

Atlanta News First called Ossoff a political “powerhouse,” comparing his denials of presidential ambition to Barack Obama’s in 2006. Bottoms, it said, would bring Georgia Democrats “unprecedented national visibility.” Both descriptions were complimentary, but only one looked toward the White House.

Presidential reputations begin taking shape long before anyone declares a candidacy, in the language we choose to describe them and the futures we allow ourselves to imagine. 

Who decided what presidential swagger was supposed to look like? El-Sayed, who said he would answer Trump’s “crass and obnoxious” politics in kind, has no intention of surrendering the stage to a bully. Ocasio-Cortez is already a serious possibility for 2028. Her fury at injustice is part of her presidential appeal.

Bottoms won an office no Black woman had ever held in a state where her ancestors were enslaved. Andrews spent years treating children whose parents worried about affording insulin and inhalers, then persuaded South Carolina to elect her. There is audacity in all of it.

How we imagine electability changes what voters do. In a 2022 study, researchers found that some Democratic primary voters hesitated to support women they preferred because they expected others to reject a woman president. Across six studies involving 7,895 participants, evidence that women received comparable electoral support to men increased willingness to support female presidential candidates. Hearing that other voters merely said they would support a woman did little.

The trap is elegant in its cruelty. We doubt a woman can win because we believe our neighbors doubt it. Each person’s caution becomes another person’s evidence.

Election Day was electric for women. Black women, who have so often done the work of delivering Democratic victories, had now made history at the top of the ticket. For the first time, more than 100 Democratic women won seats in the House alone. Across the country, women won governorships, Senate seats and the trust of voters. The next president could be among them.

I keep thinking of Bottoms at Betsy Peek’s grave, and of Sheppard’s X. The next day, Georgians chose his descendant to sign the laws of their state. 

So, by all means, let the conversation about 2028 begin. Let it be as unruly, fiery and exuberant as election night. The country has just rewritten what is possible. Why stop there? 

Flynn Coleman is an international human rights attorney, political scientist and the author of “A Human Algorithm.”

data.title: Boebert: Trump 'did some things that hurt my voters'
data.description:
Outgoing Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.) said the midterm results, which swayed overwhelmingly toward Democrats, could be a “referendum” on President Trump or the Republican Party.

“I’m not mad at the president,” Boebert said Thursday, according to The Associated Press. “The president did some things that hurt my voters.”

Boebert, who represents Colorado’s 4th Congressional District, was ousted by Democrat Eileen Laubacher earlier this month by roughly 1 percentage point, as projected by Decision Desk HQ. The forecaster leaned toward Boebert ahead of the elections.

The Colorado Republican, however, said while some of the Trump administration agenda was to blame, “I think it’s more all of us. It’s all of the Republican Party.”

 “We had solutions and we didn’t take action,” she added.

Boebert began her career in Washington in 2021, after winning in the state’s 3rd Congressional District. The following year, her political popularity became uncertain when she narrowly survived a challenge from Democrat Adam Frisch.

The Republican then announced in late 2023 that she would instead run in the more heavily GOP-favored 4th District, which was being vacated by then-retiring Rep. Ken Buck (R). She ended up winning that race by roughly 12 percentage points, securing another two years in Congress.

In 2026, her opponent raised far more than she did on the campaign trail. The lawmaker acknowledged this fact, according to the AP report.

“I didn’t raise millions of dollars and I kinda refused to,” she said. “Colorado voters know me, and, you know, if they know me enough to get rid of me, then I guess that’s my answer.”

Boebert has previously blamed policy, corruption and “markets” for the results, before the race was called. She said this year’s election was “absolutely a cry that the American people do not want corruption from anyone, any time,” adding that Americans “were played by the markets.”

“I have gas that is under $3 a gallon in my district now, when everything was closer to $6 a gallon just over a week ago,” the outgoing lawmaker continued. “And so there needs to be some accountability there. Also, we had legislation that would pause exports for diesel. We had legislation even to suspend the federal gas tax.”

data.title: Democrats weaponized AI fears for political gain, and it worked
data.description:
What an astonishing split screen! Many Americans, alarmed by an unusual series of nationwide software outages, are prepping for an AI catastrophe, even as investors charge into Anthropic’s history-making IPO, driving the AI giant’s market capitalization to a breathtaking $2 trillion.

It’s hard to imagine two more disparate messages arriving at the same moment. How could the country be so divided on the outlook for the greatest technology development in a generation?

Like everything splitting our country in two today, politics has played a role. Many smart people, including some in the industry, have voiced concerns about the fast-evolving models developed by Anthropic, Open AI and others — fears of bots crushing employment, causing a new pandemic or taking over from humans have been purposefully amplified by China-allied activists and by Democrats. But it has also been well documented that groups sympathetic to Beijing have sowed anxiety about AI and data centers, leading to efforts to slow the industry’s necessary build-out of computing power.

China is desperate to win the AI race; blocking the expansion of U.S. data centers helps its cause. 

Some communities are genuinely alarmed about data centers driving up electricity bills or leading to potential water shortages. But the widespread opposition has been totally out of proportion to the risks or costs. Polling now shows that Americans would rather live next door to a nuclear power plant than a data center, which is absurd. Politicians can and should alleviate computing campus burdens by requiring developers to generate their own power and minimize water usage.

But rather than adopt common-sense policies, Democrats chose to weaponize the issue. We know why. Thanks to Joe Biden’s unwelcome regulatory zeal, Big Tech began to shift its support to Republicans and to President Trump. CEOs like Tim Cook, Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Sundar Pichai attended Trump’s inauguration in 2025, and donated money to his campaign or inauguration fund. Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg gave a million dollars to the fund and claimed he was “very keen to play an active role” in the “president’s tech policymaking,” according to Business Insider. Amazon founder Jeff Bezos also gave a million to the inauguration, after The Washington Post helpfully declined to endorse a presidential candidate for the first time in decades. 

Democrats, threatened by the torrent of money Big Tech could throw into campaigns, began screaming about “oligarchs” taking over the country; the battle lines were drawn. Breitbart presciently predicted earlier this year that ahead of the midterms, “Americans should expect a torrent of messaging designed to heighten anxiety over real and perceived AI job losses, a plan left-leaning globalist billionaires hope will sour voters’ economic outlook and help Democrats return to power.” Spot on.  

Connecticut’s progressive Sen. Chris Murphy was just one of many Democrats living up to that expectation, telling the Bulwark last December, “There is going to be a growing appetite from voters to support candidates that are going to help them manage the potential coming disaster as AI poisons our kids and destroys all of our jobs.”   

Earlier this year, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) wrote a letter to AI executives asking them to stop pursuing new models. “It is not too late to avoid disaster,” he wrote, citing reports that AI could “lead to new bioweapons that result in the deaths of tens of millions of people.” He joined forces with Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) in September to introduce legislation that would “ban the creation of systems that humanity cannot fully control” and writing of “potential deadly consequences.”   

For months, Democrats campaigned on a platform of doom and alarmism. They warned that AI was going to gut the job market and could lead to all-out catastrophe. And it worked.

Polling showed Americans becoming more worried about AI’s impact on their lives, with an increasing number thinking the technology could do “more harm than good.” Democrats rode a tidal wave of anxiety to an historic midterm victory.  

But their fear-mongering has left Americans frightened about the future.  

Events over the last two weeks have heightened those fears. The FAA’s nationwide ground stop and outages at Microsoft, Apple, the NSA, JP Morgan Chase and United Airlines — variously described as “glitches” or “bugs” — have unsettled the country. U.S. authorities and CEOs have issued reasonable explanations for the purportedly unconnected events, but even those answers raise questions.

We are told that AI systems are uncovering software vulnerabilities at lightening speed, and that companies and institutions are responding in kind, frantically trying to patch those flaws. It makes perfect sense that such triage could lead to temporary interruptions; we have all experienced hiccups following software updates on our cellphones or TVs. But the very fact that hackers are now armed with super-capable bots that can help them invade and wreck important systems is not comforting.

Recent events may be a harbinger of things to come; no one knows. What we do know is that fear-mongering about AI became a political weapon for Democrats, independent of sober consideration of its merits or risks.   

What we also know is that AI brings the promise of extraordinary benefits in curing diseases, facilitating entrepreneurship, improving business productivity and supplementing the labor that is lost as Boomers retire.

Democrats, ever opportunistic, will moderate their antagonism to AI as tech leaders shift their allegiances (and campaign donations) back to those newly in power, and as officials welcome the revenues that data centers can offer. Count on it. 

Liz Peek is a former partner of major bracket Wall Street firm Wertheim and Company.

data.title: The collapse of Trump's blood diesel scheme is a victory for Ukraine
data.description:
President Trump triumphantly announced last month that he and Russian President Vladimir Putin had struck a deal for the U.S. to buy Russian diesel. Tankers carrying diesel departed from Russia’s Baltic Sea port of Primorsk, bound for ports on the U.S. East coast.

But they never got there. 

Some tankers veered away to South America. One steamed into the Mediterranean, and another zig-zagged aimlessly in the Atlantic. They were looking for buyers elsewhere in the world, because U.S. diesel importers, port managers and terminal operators, did not want anything to do with Russia’s “blood diesel.”

It is blood diesel the way “blood diamonds” have financed wars in West Africa. Proceeds from the deal between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin would have helped to finance Putin’s war machine, which has killed or injured tens of thousands of Ukrainian civilians, including 3,000 children, and displaced millions. 

The diesel-laden tankers were modern-day blockade runners, trying to evade U.S. and international sanctions against Russia. But the U.S. companies, under pressure from outraged senior Democrats and Republicans in Congress who claimed that the deal was illegal, passed on the diesel. They feared both reputational damage and legal jeopardy for violating the sanctions regime.  

The diesel deal was in part a political stunt, so that Trump could tell midterm voters that “lower prices for Americans is my Greatest Priority.” But the small quantity of diesel involved would have had no appreciable impact on soaring U.S. diesel prices, and voters certainly didn’t seem impressed by the deal.

In the context of Trump’s history of appeasing Putin and pushing Ukraine to make unilateral concessions, it was also a means for Trump to further pressure Ukraine into capitulation by degrading the sanctions regime. Zelensky has candidly acknowledged that “we will not prevail” if the U.S. sides with Russia, which appears to be Trump’s ambition. He has signaled that he is willing to accept most of the Kremlin’s demands to achieve peace. But a peace on Putin’s terms, which will exclude a European security force to defend Ukraine, will inevitably lead to full Russian occupation and the end of Ukrainian statehood.

That will be a peace worse than war. 

In the parts of Ukraine they have already occupied, Russian forces have detained, tortured and executed Ukrainian military officers, cultural figures and political leaders down to the village level, hunting down their targets using lists. Their “cleansing operations” have included the execution of dozens of Ukrainian priests, the banning of the Ukrainian language and the torture of journalists and writers, as both news reports and reports by international human rights groups have established. 

There is no reason to think Russian forces won’t do all of these same things throughout Ukraine, if given a chance to occupy it.

This is not the first time Russia has tried to exterminate the national identity of a prostrate country. In their infamous pact of August 1939, which set the stage for World War II, the Soviet Union aligned with Nazi Germany, and the two agreed to invade and divide Poland. While occupying the eastern half of Poland, the Soviet secret police, on Stalin’s orders, rounded up some 22,000 Polish Army officers, political leaders, police and border guards, professionals, and intellectuals and shot them — most notoriously in the Katyn Forest.

That is why the collapse of the diesel deal matters. Had the tankers offloaded Russian diesel in American ports, and American dollars started flowing to Russia, the psychological, political, and practical effects would have been devastating to Ukraine and its supporters. The war still hangs in the balance, but the failure of Trump and Putin to break the sanctions regime is a victory for Ukraine in its gallant fight for survival.

Gregory J. Wallance, a writer and former federal prosecutor, is the author of, most recently, “Into Siberia: George Kennan’s Epic Journey Through the Brutal, Frozen Heart of Russia.”

data.title: What does screentime really mean, and what's a parent to do about it?
data.description:
We have decided to raise our infant son with no screentime. I was adamant about it from way before he was born.

As someone with two older children, I certainly understand the appeal, ease and seductiveness of sticking a child in front of a screen while you get that much-needed five minutes. But as we all know, it has gone too far. I was at a “mommy and me” class recently and saw a mom holding her phone up to her child for an entire hour. It made me sad, sick and depressed all at the same time, for both of them.

But when the baby and I got home, I handed him off to my husband sitting in his easy chair, leaving them both to watching basketball. And I thought to myself: Wait, what have I just done? What exactly is a screen?

Most parents will say that a screen is the phone or iPad, but researchers mean every screen — the television in the den, the laptop for homework, the console at school, everything. And when you add it all together, the number for screentime is alarming — but the conclusions also get murky.

Children under eight years old spend an average of 2.5 hours on screens each day. That number hasn’t changed in the last six years. The difference? The device. Over 50 percent of children under eight now have their own device — a number that is way, way up. And the device has moved from the living room to the bedroom. By age two, four in 10 children have their own tablet. By age eight, one in four have their own cellphone. So the biggest question I had was whether watching television is the same as using a tablet.

The answer: It’s complicated. There are two differentiators.

The first is active versus passive viewing. Researchers separate passive watching, where the child just takes in content, from active viewing where the child interacts with a screen. A kid zoned out on cartoons is very different from a kid sounding out words with a parent beside him.

Second, the type of passive viewing — a child watching two-minute YouTube videos is in a very different position from a kid watching the Jetsons or basketball with his dad. That doesn’t change the total hours of screentime, but it has a very different result. Simply put, not all screentime is created equal.

The biggest cost of all this screentime is bedtime. More than half of children are watching screens right up until bed, against the recommendation that children need at least an hour gap between screens and sleep. It is the most damaging and the most difficult change to document.

So here’s my best advice from all the data I have seen: Pick a time that the screens go dark every night, not just for the kids but for everyone in the household. Keep all devices in the kitchen, not the bedrooms.

Just saying “no screen time” isn’t going to work and isn’t sustainable. But what you can control is when and what kind. Find old cartoons and make sure they are the original — think “Scooby Doo” or “The Jetsons” instead of the new addicting-attention deceiving versions. Have them watch old Nick-at-Nite shows like “Bewitched,” “Happy Days,” or “I Love Lucy.” Have them watch sports.

Stop the screens from being small and in the bedrooms and go back to family TV-watching. Screens can actually be good family bonding time.  And never, ever allow screens at meal times. Some people argue that no screen is morally superior to other screens. But research and common sense show that they are wrong.

This all goes for parents too. While I was writing this article, I looked at my own screentime. It made me feel sick, especially when I added up how much time over the course of my life I am spending and wasting on my screen. I don’t think I’m alone in that.

Dr. Liberty Vittert Capito is a professor of the practice of data science at the Olin Business School at Washington University in St. Louis. She is co-host of the Harvard Data Science Review podcast and the MIT data science podcast.
